title: Veil of Ignorance Pricing
equation: Fairness Score = Acceptability to Both Sides ÷ 10
hook: If you'd hate being on the other side of your own policy, it's probably not fair.
statement: Set policies you'd still accept even if you didn't know which side of them you'd end up on.
explainer: Pretend you could end up as the customer, the vendor, or the employee under your rule. If you'd still sign off on it, it's fair. If not, it's just self-serving.
sop: Write down the policy and everyone it affects.
Imagine you don't know which of those seats you'll be in.
Rate Acceptability to Both Sides from 1 to 10.
Divide by 10 and rewrite anything that only works from your seat.
Publish it and hold yourself to it.
equation_example: A refund policy scores 8 for Acceptability to Both Sides. 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8, a fair rule most people would accept. A one-sided clause scoring 3 gives 0.3, so rewrite it. Higher works from any seat. Lower only serves you.
question: Read your refund or cancellation policy as if you were the customer. Rewrite one line.
closing_statement: Build rules you'd accept from the weakest seat.
caption:
Principle Nº 365: Veil of Ignorance Pricing

If you'd hate being on the other side of your own policy, it's probably not fair.

Set policies you'd still accept even if you didn't know which side of them you'd end up on.

Your turn: Read your refund or cancellation policy as if you were the customer. Rewrite one line.
